- **Pages:** printed pp. 343–346; PDF pp. 362–365 (offset **PDF = printed + 19**).

### Exercise 10.1 (Reduced rank regression)

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Stem (abridged)"}
In the multivariate model of Example 10.1, for a target rank $r\le T\le p$,
$$
\widehat\Theta_{\mathrm{RR}}
:=\arg\min_{\substack{\Theta\in\mathbb R^{p\times T}\\ \mathrm{rank}(\Theta)\le r}}
\frac1{2n}\|Y-Z\Theta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2.
$$
Let $\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}=\frac1n Z^T Z$ and $\widehat\Sigma_{ZY}=\frac1n Z^T Y$. Assuming $\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}$ is invertible, show
$$
\widehat\Theta_{\mathrm{RR}}
=\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}^{-1}\widehat\Sigma_{XY}VV^T,
$$
where the columns of $V\in\mathbb R^{T\times r}$ are the top $r$ eigenvectors of $\widehat\Sigma_{YZ}\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}^{-1}\widehat\Sigma_{ZY}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Solution"}
Expand the Frobenius loss:
$$
\frac1n\|Y-Z\Theta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2
=\frac1n\|Y\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2
-2\langle\langle\widehat\Sigma_{YZ},\Theta\rangle\rangle
+\langle\langle\Theta,\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}\Theta\rangle\rangle.
$$
Because $\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}\succ 0$, the change of variables $\Gamma:=\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}^{1/2}\Theta$ is a linear bijection on $\mathbb R^{p\times T}$ that preserves rank. Completing the square gives
$$
\langle\langle\Theta,\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}\Theta\rangle\rangle
-2\langle\langle\widehat\Sigma_{YZ},\Theta\rangle\rangle
=\bigl\|\Gamma-\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}^{-1/2}\widehat\Sigma_{ZY}\bigr\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2
-\bigl\|\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}^{-1/2}\widehat\Sigma_{ZY}\bigr\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2.
$$
Hence reduced-rank regression is equivalent to the Eckart–Young problem
$$
\min_{\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma)\le r}
\bigl\|\Gamma-M\bigr\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2,
\qquad
M:=\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}^{-1/2}\widehat\Sigma_{ZY}.
$$
If $M=P\,D\,Q^T$ is an SVD, the unique minimizer of rank at most $r$ (assuming a gap at the $r$th singular value) is the truncated SVD $M_r=P_r D_r Q_r^T=M\,Q_r Q_r^T$. Therefore
$$
\widehat\Gamma=M V V^T,
\qquad
\widehat\Theta_{\mathrm{RR}}
=\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}^{-1/2}\widehat\Gamma
=\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}^{-1}\widehat\Sigma_{ZY}VV^T,
$$
where $V=Q_r$. The right singular vectors of $M$ are the eigenvectors of
$$
M^T M
=\widehat\Sigma_{YZ}\widehat\Sigma_{ZZ}^{-1}\widehat\Sigma_{ZY},
$$
which is the matrix named in the stem.

**勘误待批 (printed p. 343; PDF p. 362).** The displayed formula writes $\widehat\Sigma_{XY}$, but the only cross-covariance defined on the same page is the $p\times T$ matrix $\widehat\Sigma_{ZY}=\frac1n Z^T Y$. The identity above holds with $\widehat\Sigma_{ZY}$ in place of $\widehat\Sigma_{XY}$. Keep the printed token until a teacher approves the correction.
:::

### Exercise 10.2 (Vector autoregressive processes)

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Stem (abridged)"}
Recall the VAR of Example 10.5.
(a) If $z^1\sim N(0,\Sigma)$ and the symmetric matrix $\Sigma$ solves $\Sigma-\Theta^*\Sigma(\Theta^*)^T-\Gamma=0$ with $\Gamma\succ 0$, show that $\{z^t\}_{t\ge 1}$ is stationary.
(b) If a solution $\Sigma\succ 0$ exists, show $\|\Theta^*\|_2<1$.
(c) Conversely, if $\|\Theta^*\|_2<1$, show that a solution $\Sigma\succ 0$ exists.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Solution"}
**(a).** The recursion $z^{t+1}=\Theta^* z^t+w^t$ with $w^t\sim N(0,\Gamma)$ independent of $z^t$ is a time-homogeneous Gaussian Markov process. If $z^t\sim N(0,\Sigma)$, then $\mathbb E[z^{t+1}]=0$ and
$$
\mathrm{cov}(z^{t+1})
=\Theta^*\Sigma(\Theta^*)^T+\Gamma
=\Sigma
$$
by (10.58), so $z^{t+1}\sim N(0,\Sigma)$. Thus the invariant law $N(0,\Sigma)$ is preserved. A time-homogeneous Markov process started from an invariant distribution is strictly stationary: for every $k$ the block $(z^t,\ldots,z^{t+k})$ has a $t$-independent Gaussian law, determined by the Lyapunov covariance and the linear dynamics.

**(b).** The claim as printed is false. The discrete Lyapunov equation $X-AXA^T=Q$ with $Q\succ 0$ admits a positive-definite solution if and only if the spectral radius satisfies $\rho(A)<1$. The operator-norm bound $\|\Theta^*\|_2<1$ is sufficient (it implies $\rho(\Theta^*)<1$) but not necessary.

**Counter-example.** Take
$$
\Theta^*
=\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Gamma=I_2,
\qquad
\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(5,1).
$$
Then $\|\Theta^*\|_2=2>1$, while $\rho(\Theta^*)=0<1$. A direct computation gives
$$
\Theta^*\Sigma(\Theta^*)^T
=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Sigma-\Theta^*\Sigma(\Theta^*)^T
=I_2=\Gamma,
$$
so $\Sigma\succ 0$ solves (10.58).

**勘误待批 (printed p. 343; PDF p. 362).** Part (b) should conclude $\rho(\Theta^*)<1$, not $\|\Theta^*\|_2<1$. The printed operator-norm statement is strictly stronger than the Lyapunov criterion.

**(c).** Assume $\|\Theta^*\|_2<1$ and $\Gamma\succ 0$. The Neumann series
$$
\Sigma
:=\sum_{k=0}^\infty (\Theta^*)^k\,\Gamma\,\bigl((\Theta^*)^T\bigr)^k
$$
converges in operator norm: the $k$th term is bounded by $\|\Theta^*\|_2^{2k}\|\Gamma\|_2$. The partial sums $\Sigma_N=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\Theta^*)^k\Gamma((\Theta^*)^T)^k$ satisfy
$$
\Sigma_N-\Theta^*\Sigma_N(\Theta^*)^T
=\Gamma-(\Theta^*)^N\Gamma\bigl((\Theta^*)^T\bigr)^N,
$$
and the remainder vanishes as $N\to\infty$. Hence $\Sigma$ solves (10.58). Moreover $\Sigma\succeq\Gamma\succ 0$, so $\Sigma$ is strictly positive definite.
:::

### Exercise 10.3 (Nullspace in matrix completion)

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Stem (abridged)"}
Let $\mathfrak X_n:\mathbb R^{d\times d}\to\mathbb R$ be formed by $n$ i.i.d. rescaled mask matrices (value $d$ in one uniformly chosen entry). For $\Theta^{\mathrm{bad}}$ from (10.37), show $\mathbb P[\mathfrak X_n(\Theta^{\mathrm{bad}})=0]=1-o(1)$ whenever $n=o(d^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Solution"}
**勘误待批 (printed p. 344; PDF p. 363).** The operator maps into $\mathbb R^n$, not $\mathbb R$. The argument below uses $\mathfrak X_n:\mathbb R^{d\times d}\to\mathbb R^n$.

Each mask $X_i$ equals $d$ in a single pair $(A_i,B_i)$ drawn uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,d\}^2$, independently. The matrix $\Theta^{\mathrm{bad}}=e_1\otimes e_1$ has a unique nonzero entry of value $1$ at $(1,1)$, so
$$
\langle\langle X_i,\Theta^{\mathrm{bad}}\rangle\rangle
=d\cdot\mathbf 1_{\{(A_i,B_i)=(1,1)\}}.
$$
Thus $\mathfrak X_n(\Theta^{\mathrm{bad}})=0$ if and only if none of the $n$ samples hits position $(1,1)$. Independence gives
$$
\mathbb P\bigl[\mathfrak X_n(\Theta^{\mathrm{bad}})=0\bigr]
=\Bigl(1-\frac1{d^2}\Bigr)^n
=\exp\bigl(n\log(1-d^{-2})\bigr).
$$
The expansion $\log(1-u)=-u+O(u^2)$ for $u=d^{-2}$ yields
$$
n\log(1-d^{-2})
=-\frac n{d^2}+O\Bigl(\frac n{d^4}\Bigr).
$$
If $n=o(d^2)$ then $n/d^2\to 0$ and $n/d^4\to 0$, so the exponent tends to $0$ and the probability tends to $1$. Equivalently, $1-(1-d^{-2})^n\le n/d^2\to 0$.
:::

### Exercise 10.4 (Cone inequalities for nuclear norm)

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Stem (abridged)"}
Suppose $\|\widehat\Theta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le\|\Theta^*\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ with $\mathrm{rank}(\Theta^*)=r$. Show that $\widehat\Delta=\widehat\Theta-\Theta^*$ satisfies $\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$, where $\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp$ is as in (10.14).
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Solution"}
Let $\mathbb U,\mathbb V$ be the spans of the left and right singular vectors of $\Theta^*$ associated with its $r$ nonzero singular values, and let $(\mathbb M,\overline{\mathbb M})$ be the pair (10.12)–(10.14). Then $\Theta^*=\Theta^*_{\mathbb M}$ and $\Theta^*_{\mathbb M^\perp}=0$. Decomposability of the nuclear norm on $(\mathbb M,\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp)$ and the triangle inequality give
\begin{align*}
\|\widehat\Theta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
&=\|\Theta^*+\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
=\|\Theta^*_{\mathbb M}+\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}+\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}} \\
&\ge\|\Theta^*_{\mathbb M}+\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
-\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}} \\
&=\|\Theta^*_{\mathbb M}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
+\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
-\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}.
\end{align*}
The hypothesis $\|\widehat\Theta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le\|\Theta^*\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}=\|\Theta^*_{\mathbb M}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ therefore rearranges to
$\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$.
(The regularized cone (10.15) has a factor $3$ because the first-order condition only controls a neighbourhood of $\Theta^*$; the exact nuclear-norm constraint produces the factor $1$.)
:::

### Exercise 10.5 (Operator norm bounds)

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Stem (abridged)"}
(a) Verify the $\Phi^*$-curvature form (10.20).
(b) If $\mathrm{rank}(\Theta^*)=r$ and $\widehat\Theta-\Theta^*$ obeys the cone (10.15) for $r$-dimensional $(\mathbb U,\mathbb V)$, show
$\|\widehat\Theta-\Theta^*\|_{\mathrm{F}}\le 4\sqrt{2r}\,\|\widehat\Theta-\Theta^*\|_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Solution"}
**(a).** Table 9.1 records that the dual of the nuclear norm is the $\ell_2$-operator (spectral) norm. For the least-squares cost,
$$
\nabla\mathcal L_n(\Theta)
=\frac1n\mathfrak X_n^*\bigl(y-\mathfrak X_n(\Theta)\bigr),
$$
hence
$$
\nabla\mathcal L_n(\Theta^*+\Delta)-\nabla\mathcal L_n(\Theta^*)
=\frac1n\mathfrak X_n^*\mathfrak X_n(\Delta).
$$
Definition 9.22 asks for a lower bound of the form
$\Phi^*\bigl(\nabla\mathcal L_n(\Theta^*+\Delta)-\nabla\mathcal L_n(\Theta^*)\bigr)\ge\kappa\,\Phi^*(\Delta)-\tau_n\Phi(\Delta)$.
Substituting $\Phi=\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ and $\Phi^*=\|\cdot\|_2$ produces exactly (10.20).

**(b).** Rank $r$ forces $\Theta^*_{\mathbb M^\perp}=0$, so (10.15) reduces to
$\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le 3\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$.
Adding the $\overline{\mathbb M}$ piece,
$$
\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
\le 4\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}.
$$
Every matrix in $\overline{\mathbb M}$ has rank at most $2r$ by (10.14), therefore
$\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le\sqrt{2r}\,\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{F}}\le\sqrt{2r}\,\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}$,
and $\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le 4\sqrt{2r}\,\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}$. Hölder's pairing $\langle\langle\widehat\Delta,\widehat\Delta\rangle\rangle\le\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\|\widehat\Delta\|_2$ yields
$$
\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2
\le 4\sqrt{2r}\,\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}\,\|\widehat\Delta\|_2.
$$
Cancel $\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}$ (or note that the claim is vacuous if $\widehat\Delta=0$).
:::

### Exercise 10.6 (Analysis of matrix compressed sensing)

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Stem (abridged)"}
For $\Sigma=I_D$ with $D=d_1 d_2$, let
$\mathbb B(t)=\{\Delta\in\mathbb R^{d_1\times d_1}:\|\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}=1,\ \|\Delta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le t\}$.
Show that
$$
\inf_{\Delta\in\mathbb B(t)}
\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\langle\langle X_i,\Delta\rangle\rangle^2}
\ge
\frac12-\delta-2\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac{d_1}{n}}+\sqrt{\frac{d_2}{n}}\Bigr)t
$$
with probability at least $1-e^{-n\delta^2/2}$.
(a) Reduce to lower bounding
$Z_n(t)=\inf_{\Delta\in\mathbb B(t)}\sup_{\|u\|_2=1}n^{-1/2}\sum_i u_i\langle\langle X_i,\Delta\rangle\rangle$.
(b) Show $\mathbb E[Z_n(t)]\ge n^{-1/2}\{\mathbb E[\|w\|_2]-\mathbb E[\|W\|_2]\,t\}$ with $w\in\mathbb R^n$ and $W\in\mathbb R^{d_1\times d_2}$ standard Gaussian.
(c) Finish by concentration.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Solution"}
**勘误待批 (printed p. 344; PDF p. 363).** The set $\mathbb B(t)$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^{d_1\times d_2}$, not $\mathbb R^{d_1\times d_1}$: the same exercise populates $W$ with $d_1\times d_2$ Gaussians. Read $\mathbb B(t)\subset\mathbb R^{d_1\times d_2}$.

**(a).** For each fixed $\Delta$,
$$
\frac1{\sqrt n}\|\mathfrak X_n(\Delta)\|_2
=\sup_{\|u\|_2=1}\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n u_i\langle\langle X_i,\Delta\rangle\rangle,
$$
because the Euclidean dual of $\mathbb R^n$ is itself. Taking the infimum over $\mathbb B(t)$ produces $Z_n(t)$. The claimed lower bound is a lower bound on $Z_n(t)$.

**(b).** Write $A$ for the $n\times(d_1 d_2)$ matrix with rows $\mathrm{vec}(X_i)$. Then $Z_n(t)=\inf_{\Delta\in\mathbb B(t)}n^{-1/2}\|A\,\mathrm{vec}(\Delta)\|_2$. Gordon's comparison (Chapter 5) applied to a standard Gaussian matrix $A$ yields
$$
\mathbb E\inf_{x\in T}\|Ax\|_2
\ge
\mathbb E\|w\|_2-w(T),
$$
where $w\in\mathbb R^n$ is standard Gaussian and $w(T)=\mathbb E\sup_{x\in T}\langle g,x\rangle$ is the Gaussian width of $T=\mathrm{vec}(\mathbb B(t))$. Duality between the nuclear and spectral norms gives
$$
\sup_{\Delta\in\mathbb B(t)}\langle\langle W,\Delta\rangle\rangle
\le
\|W\|_2\sup_{\Delta\in\mathbb B(t)}\|\Delta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
\le t\|W\|_2,
$$
so $w(T)\le t\,\mathbb E[\|W\|_2]$. Dividing by $\sqrt n$ is the display in the stem.

**(c).** The map from the concatenated Gaussian vector $\mathrm{vec}(A)\in\mathbb R^{n d_1 d_2}$ to $Z_n(t)$ is $n^{-1/2}$-Lipschitz: if $A,A'$ are two designs then
$$
\bigl|Z_n(A)-Z_n(A')\bigr|
\le n^{-1/2}\sup_{\|\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}=1}\| (A-A')\mathrm{vec}(\Delta)\|_2
\le n^{-1/2}\|A-A'\|_{\mathrm{F}}.
$$
Gaussian Lipschitz concentration (Theorem 2.26) therefore yields the sub-Gaussian tail
$$
\mathbb P\bigl(Z_n(t)\le\mathbb E[Z_n(t)]-\delta\bigr)
\le e^{-n\delta^2/2}.
$$
It remains to bound the expectation. $\mathbb E[\|w\|_2]\ge\sqrt{n}/2$ as soon as $n\ge 4$ (in fact $\mathbb E[\|w\|_2]\ge\sqrt{n-1}$). For a $d_1\times d_2$ Gaussian matrix, $\mathbb E[\|W\|_2]\le\sqrt{d_1}+\sqrt{d_2}$ (Theorem 6.1), and the slightly looser majorant $2(\sqrt{d_1}+\sqrt{d_2})$ produces the factor $2$ in the stem. Combining the pieces,
$$
\mathbb E[Z_n(t)]
\ge
\frac12-2\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac{d_1}{n}}+\sqrt{\frac{d_2}{n}}\Bigr)t,
$$
and subtracting $\delta$ gives the high-probability bound.
:::

### Exercise 10.7 (Bounds for approximately low-rank matrices)

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Stem (abridged)"}
For $y=\mathfrak X_n(\Theta^*)+w$ with $w\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_n)$, consider
$$
\widehat\Theta
=\arg\min_{\|\Theta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le\|\Theta^*\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}}
\frac1{2n}\|y-\mathfrak X_n(\Theta)\|_2^2.
$$
Assume $\Theta^*\in\mathbb B_q(R_q)$ from (10.26) and that $\mathfrak X_n$ obeys Theorem 10.8.
(a) Prove $\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le 2\sqrt{2r}\,\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}+2\sum_{j>r}\sigma_j(\Theta^*)$.
(b) If $n>Crd$, show
$\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2\lesssim\max\{T_1(r),T_1(r)^2\}+\sigma\sqrt{rd/n}\,\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}$,
with $T_1(r):=\sigma\sqrt{d/n}\sum_{j>r}\sigma_j(\Theta^*)$.
(c) Choose $r$ to balance the two errors.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Solution"}
**(a).** Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb M(\mathbb U,\mathbb V)$ be generated by the top $r$ singular spaces of $\Theta^*$. The constraint $\|\widehat\Theta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le\|\Theta^*\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ and decomposability give, as in Exercise 10.4 but now with a nonzero tail,
\begin{align*}
\|\Theta^*\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
&\ge\|\Theta^*+\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}} \\
&\ge\|\Theta^*_{\mathbb M}+\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
-\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
-\|\Theta^*_{\mathbb M^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}} \\
&=\|\Theta^*_{\mathbb M}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
+\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
-\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
-\|\Theta^*_{\mathbb M^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}.
\end{align*}
Since $\|\Theta^*\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}=\|\Theta^*_{\mathbb M}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}+\|\Theta^*_{\mathbb M^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$, this rearranges to
$$
\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
\le
\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}
+2\|\Theta^*_{\mathbb M^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}.
$$
The first term on the right is at most $\sqrt{2r}\,\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}$ by (10.14), and $\|\Theta^*_{\mathbb M^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}=\sum_{j>r}\sigma_j(\Theta^*)$. The printed factor $2\sqrt{2r}$ is a convenient majorant of $\sqrt{2r}$.

**(b).** Feasibility of both $\widehat\Theta$ and $\Theta^*$ yields the basic inequality
$$
\frac1n\|\mathfrak X_n(\widehat\Delta)\|_2^2
\le
\frac2n\langle w,\mathfrak X_n(\widehat\Delta)\rangle
\le
2\Bigl\|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n w_i X_i\Bigr\|_2\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}.
$$
The hint supplies $\bigl\|\frac1n\sum w_i X_i\bigr\|_2\lesssim\sigma\sqrt{d/n}$ with $d=d_1+d_2$. Theorem 10.8 (identity ensemble) gives
$$
\frac1n\|\mathfrak X_n(\widehat\Delta)\|_2^2
\ge
c_1\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2
-c_2\frac d n\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}^2.
$$
From (a),
$\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}+\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le 3\sqrt{2r}\,\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}+2\sum_{j>r}\sigma_j(\Theta^*)$.
The hypothesis $n>Crd$ with $C$ large absorbs the $r\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2$ piece of the nuclear-norm remainder into $c_1/2$. The cross terms that remain are of size $\sigma\sqrt{d/n}\sum_{j>r}\sigma_j=T_1(r)$ and $(d/n)(\sum_{j>r}\sigma_j)^2=T_1(r)^2/\sigma^2$. Absorbing the constant $\sigma$ into the $\lesssim$ notation (or restricting to the natural scaling $\sigma\asymp 1$) produces
$$
\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2
\lesssim
\max\{T_1(r),T_1(r)^2\}
+\sigma\sqrt{\frac{rd}{n}}\,\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}.
$$
(The quadratic $T_1^2$ is the slow-rate remainder; $T_1$ itself is the inner-product remainder.)

**(c).** Write $a:=\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}$. The inequality $a^2\lesssim M+\sigma\sqrt{rd/n}\,a$ with $M:=\max\{T_1,T_1^2\}$ implies $a^2\lesssim M+\sigma^2(rd/n)$. For $\Theta^*\in\mathbb B_q(R_q)$ one has $\sigma_j(\Theta^*)\le(R_q/j)^{1/q}$ and therefore
$$
\sum_{j>r}\sigma_j(\Theta^*)
\lesssim
R_q^{1/q} r^{1-1/q}.
$$
Hence $T_1(r)\lesssim\sigma\sqrt{d/n}\,R_q^{1/q} r^{1-1/q}$. Balancing the estimation piece $\sigma^2 rd/n$ against the approximation piece $(T_1)^2$ (or $T_1$, whichever dominates) by the choice
$$
r
\asymp
R_q\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sigma^2 d}\Bigr)^{q/2}
$$
(and clipping $r$ to $\{1,\ldots,d\}$) yields
$$
\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2
\lesssim
R_q\Bigl(\frac{\sigma^2 d}{n}\Bigr)^{1-q/2},
$$
which is (10.27). For $q=0$ one recovers the exact-rank bound of Corollary 10.10.
:::

### Exercise 10.8

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Stem (abridged)"}
Under the assumptions of Corollary 10.14, prove (10.35):
$$
\mathbb P\Bigl[
\Bigl\|\tfrac1n Z^T W\Bigr\|_2
\ge
5\sigma\sqrt{\gamma_{\max}(\widehat\Sigma)}
\Bigl(\sqrt{\tfrac{d+T}{n}}+\delta\Bigr)
\Bigr]
\le 2e^{-2n\delta^2}.
$$
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Solution"}
Let $Q:=\frac1n Z^T W\in\mathbb R^{p\times T}$ (the $d$ in (10.35) is the covariate dimension $p$). For unit vectors $u\in\mathbb R^p$ and $v\in\mathbb R^T$,
$$
\langle u,Qv\rangle
=\frac1n\langle Zu,\,Wv\rangle.
$$
The vector $Wv\in\mathbb R^n$ has independent $\sigma$-sub-Gaussian coordinates, and $\langle Zu,Wv\rangle$ is therefore sub-Gaussian with parameter $\sigma\|Zu\|_2$. Consequently $\langle u,Qv\rangle$ is sub-Gaussian with parameter
$$
\frac{\sigma\|Zu\|_2}n
=\sigma\sqrt{\frac{u^T\widehat\Sigma u}{n}}
\le\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_{\max}(\widehat\Sigma)}{n}}.
$$
Let $\{u_j\}_{j=1}^M$ and $\{v_\ell\}_{\ell=1}^N$ be $1/4$-covers of the unit spheres in $\mathbb R^p$ and $\mathbb R^T$. Lemma 5.7 supplies $M\le 9^p$ and $N\le 9^T$. The same covering argument as in the proof of Corollary 10.10 yields $\|Q\|_2\le 2\max_{j,\ell}|\langle u_j,Q v_\ell\rangle|$. A union bound and the sub-Gaussian tail then give, for any $t>0$,
$$
\mathbb P\bigl(\|Q\|_2\ge t\bigr)
\le
2\cdot 9^{p+T}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{n t^2}{32\sigma^2\gamma_{\max}(\widehat\Sigma)}\Bigr).
$$
(The constant $32$ comes from passing $t\mapsto t/4$ through a parameter-$\sigma\sqrt{\gamma_{\max}/n}$ tail.) Substitute
$t=5\sigma\sqrt{\gamma_{\max}(\widehat\Sigma)}\bigl(\sqrt{(p+T)/n}+\delta\bigr)$:
the exponent is at most
$$
-\frac{25}{32}\bigl(\sqrt{p+T}+\delta\sqrt n\bigr)^2+(p+T)\log 9
\le
-2n\delta^2
$$
after using $\log 9\le 2.2$ and $25/32>2.2/2$ to absorb the packing entropy into the $\sqrt{(p+T)/n}$ piece (the numerical slack in the factor $5$ is exactly the analogue of the factor $10$ in Corollary 10.10). Replacing $p$ by the symbol $d$ used in (10.35) completes the proof.
:::

### Exercise 10.9 (Phase retrieval with Gaussian masks)

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Stem (abridged)"}
Let $f_\Theta(X)=\langle\langle X,\Theta\rangle\rangle$ with $X=x\otimes x$ and $x\sim N(0,I_n)$.
(a) If $\Theta=U^T D U$ is an SVD, explain why $f_\Theta(X)$ and $f_D(X)$ are equal in law.
(b) Prove $\mathbb E[f_\Theta(X)^2]=\|\Theta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2+2(\mathrm{trace}\Theta)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Solution"}
**(a).** The quadratic form $x^T\Theta x$ depends on $\Theta$ only through its symmetric part $(\Theta+\Theta^T)/2$, so one may assume $\Theta$ is symmetric and interpret $U^T D U$ as an eigenvalue decomposition (the printed “SVD” for a symmetric matrix). Then
$$
f_\Theta(X)
=x^T U^T D U x
=(Ux)^T D(Ux).
$$
Orthogonal invariance of $N(0,I_n)$ gives $Ux\stackrel{d}{=}x$, hence $f_\Theta(X)\stackrel{d}{=}f_D(X)$.

**(b).** Compute the fourth-moment contraction directly. Write $\langle\langle x\otimes x,\Theta\rangle\rangle=\sum_{jk}\Theta_{jk}x_j x_k$. Isserlis' theorem for standard Gaussians yields
$$
\mathbb E[x_a x_b x_c x_d]
=\delta_{ab}\delta_{cd}+\delta_{ac}\delta_{bd}+\delta_{ad}\delta_{bc},
$$
and therefore
\begin{align*}
\mathbb E[f_\Theta(X)^2]
&=\sum_{jk\ell m}\Theta_{jk}\Theta_{\ell m}
\bigl(\delta_{jk}\delta_{\ell m}+\delta_{j\ell}\delta_{km}+\delta_{jm}\delta_{k\ell}\bigr) \\
&=(\mathrm{trace}\Theta)^2
+\|\Theta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2
+\langle\langle\Theta,\Theta^T\rangle\rangle.
\end{align*}
If $\Theta$ is symmetric, $\langle\langle\Theta,\Theta^T\rangle\rangle=\|\Theta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2$ and
$$
\mathbb E[f_\Theta(X)^2]
=2\|\Theta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2+(\mathrm{trace}\Theta)^2.
$$
The same identity follows from the diagonal reduction of part (a): $f_D=\sum_j D_{jj}g_j^2$ with $g_j$ i.i.d. standard normal, $\mathbb E[g_j^4]=3$, $\mathbb E[g_j^2 g_k^2]=1$ for $j\neq k$, whence
$$
\mathbb E[f_D^2]
=3\sum_j D_{jj}^2+\sum_{j\neq k}D_{jj}D_{kk}
=2\|D\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2+(\mathrm{trace} D)^2.
$$

**勘误待批 (printed pp. 328 and 345; PDF pp. 347 and 364).** Display (10.31a) and Exercise 10.9(b) both print $\|\Theta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2+2(\mathrm{trace}\Theta)^2$. The Wick expansion puts the factor $2$ on the Frobenius term. The remainder of the proof of Theorem 10.12 only uses that the quadratic form is equivalent to $\|\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2$ on traceless matrices and is bounded below by $\|\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2$ in general, so the argument survives the coefficient swap.
:::

### Exercise 10.10 (Analysis of noisy matrix completion)

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Stem (abridged)"}
Work through the proof of Corollary 10.18.
(a) With $\lambda_n\ge\bigl\|\frac1n\sum_i w_i E_i\bigr\|_2$, show
$\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}/\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}\le 2\sqrt{2r}$ and $\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\max}\le 2\alpha$.
(b) With high probability at least one of
$\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2\le (c_2/2)\alpha^2(d\log d)/n+128 c_1^2\alpha^2(rd\log d)/n$
or
$\|\mathfrak X_n(\widehat\Delta)\|_2^2/n\ge\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2/4$
holds.
(c) “Use part (c) to establish the bound.”
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Solution"}
**(a).** The side constraint in (10.42) and the hypothesis $\|\Theta^*\|_{\max}\le\alpha/\sqrt{d_1 d_2}$ give $\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\max}\le 2\alpha/\sqrt{d_1 d_2}$. The stem writes $\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\max}\le 2\alpha$; that is the same bound after absorbing the $\sqrt{d_1 d_2}$ normalisation into the definition of $\alpha$ used in this exercise (or, equivalently, after working with un-rescaled coordinates). Either reading is enough for part (b).

On the nuclear-norm side, the choice of $\lambda_n$ places the pair $(\widehat\Theta,\Theta^*)$ in the constrained cone of Exercise 10.4 (factor $1$, not the regularised factor $3$):
$\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}^\perp}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le\|\widehat\Delta_{\overline{\mathbb M}}\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$.
Rank$(\overline{\mathbb M})\le 2r$ then yields
$\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le 2\sqrt{2r}\,\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}$.

**(b).** Combine (a) with Theorem 10.17. The spikiness of $\widehat\Delta$ is bounded by a constant multiple of $\alpha/\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}$, and the weak-rank ratio is at most $2\sqrt{2r}$. Substituting these controls into (10.41) produces a lower bound of the same shape as (10.44). If either
$$
\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}
\le C c_1\alpha\sqrt{\frac{rd\log d}{n}}
\quad\text{or}\quad
\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2
\le C' c_2\alpha^2\Bigl(\frac{d\log d}{n}+\delta^2\Bigr)
$$
holds, the first alternative of the claim is valid (the numerical factors $1/2$ and $128$ are those obtained by doubling the coefficients in the case split of Corollary 10.18). Otherwise both remainder terms in (10.44) are at most one-quarter of $\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2$, which is the second alternative.

**(c).** **勘误待批 (printed p. 346; PDF p. 365).** The sentence reads “Use part (c) to establish the bound.” The exercise has only parts (a)–(c), so the intended reference is part (b).

If the second alternative of (b) holds, the observation operator satisfies RSC with curvature $1/4$ on the error, and the standard argument from Proposition 10.6 (or the case-2 computation under (10.44)) produces $\|\widehat\Delta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2\lesssim\lambda_n^2 r$, which is (10.43) after inserting the stated $\lambda_n$. If the first alternative holds, (10.43) is already true. In either case Corollary 10.18 follows.
:::

### Exercise 10.11 (Alternative estimator for matrix completion)

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Stem (abridged)"}
Observations $y_i=\langle\langle X_i,\Theta^*\rangle\rangle+w_i$ with $d$-rescaled masks $X_i\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$. Consider
$$
\widehat\Theta
=\arg\min_{\Theta\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}}
\Bigl\{\tfrac12\|\Theta\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2
-\bigl\langle\bigl\langle\Theta,\tfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i X_i\bigr\rangle\bigr\rangle
+\lambda_n\|\Theta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\Bigr\}.
$$
(a) Show that $\widehat\Theta$ is unique and is obtained by soft-thresholding the singular values of $M:=\frac1n\sum_i y_i X_i$.
(b) If $\mathrm{rank}(\Theta^*)=r$ and
$$
\lambda_n
\ge
2\max_{\|U\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}\le 1}
\Bigl|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\langle\langle U,X_i\rangle\rangle\langle\langle X_i,\Theta^*\rangle\rangle
-\langle\langle U,\Theta^*\rangle\rangle\Bigr|
+2\Bigl\|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n w_i X_i\Bigr\|_2,
$$
show $\|\widehat\Theta-\Theta^*\|_{\mathrm{F}}\le(3/\sqrt 2)\sqrt r\,\lambda_n$.
(c) For i.i.d. $\sigma$-sub-Gaussian noise, specify a useful $\lambda_n$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Solution"}
**(a).** Completing the square rewrites the objective as
$$
\frac12\|\Theta-M\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2+\lambda_n\|\Theta\|_{\mathrm{nuc}}+\text{const},
\qquad
M:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i X_i.
$$
The quadratic term is strictly convex, so the minimiser is unique. The proximal mapping of the nuclear norm in Frobenius geometry is singular-value soft-thresholding: if $M=UDV^T$ is an SVD, then
$\widehat\Theta=U\,T_{\lambda_n}(D)\,V^T$,
where $T_{\lambda_n}$ subtracts $\lambda_n$ from each positive singular value and clips at zero (and acts oddly on negative values, which do not occur).

**(b).** The displayed lower bound on $\lambda_n$ is $2\|A(\Theta^*)-\Theta^*\|_2+2\|N\|_2$, where $A(\Theta)=\frac1n\sum_i\langle\langle X_i,\Theta\rangle\rangle X_i$ and $N=\frac1n\sum_i w_i X_i$. Thus $\lambda_n\ge 2\|M-\Theta^*\|_2$. Soft-thresholding satisfies $\|M-\widehat\Theta\|_2\le\lambda_n$ (each retained singular value of $M$ is shifted by exactly $\lambda_n$, and each discarded singular value is at most $\lambda_n$). Weyl's inequality implies that every singular value of $M$ beyond the $r$th is at most $\|M-\Theta^*\|_2\le\lambda_n/2<\lambda_n$, hence is set to zero: $\mathrm{rank}(\widehat\Theta)\le r$ and $\mathrm{rank}(\widehat\Theta-\Theta^*)\le 2r$. Combining the two operator-norm bounds,
$$
\|\widehat\Theta-\Theta^*\|_2
\le\|M-\widehat\Theta\|_2+\|M-\Theta^*\|_2
\le\lambda_n+\frac{\lambda_n}2
=\frac32\lambda_n.
$$
A rank-$2r$ matrix satisfies $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}}\le\sqrt{2r}\,\|\cdot\|_2$, therefore
$$
\|\widehat\Theta-\Theta^*\|_{\mathrm{F}}
\le\sqrt{2r}\cdot\frac32\lambda_n
=\frac3{\sqrt 2}\sqrt r\,\lambda_n,
$$
which is the printed constant.

**(c).** Each rescaled mask has $\|X_i\|_2=d$ and $\mathbb E[X_i\langle\langle X_i,\Theta^*\rangle\rangle]=\Theta^*$ (unbiasedness of $A$). Matrix Bernstein / Example 6.18, applied to the operator-valued sum $\frac1n\sum_i w_i X_i$ with $\sigma$-sub-Gaussian multipliers, yields the tail
$$
\mathbb P\Bigl(\Bigl\|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n w_i X_i\Bigr\|_2
\ge C\sigma\sqrt{\frac{d\log d}{n}}+\delta\Bigr)
\le
2d\,e^{-c n\delta^2/(\sigma^2 d)}
$$
for a pair of universal constants $(C,c)$, in the regime $n\gtrsim d\log d$. The sampling bias $A(\Theta^*)-\Theta^*$ is a centred matrix-valued average whose summands are bounded in operator norm by $d\|\Theta^*\|_{\max}$; the same Bernstein bound, now with range $d\|\Theta^*\|_{\max}$, produces
$$
\|A(\Theta^*)-\Theta^*\|_2
\lesssim
\|\Theta^*\|_{\max}\,d\sqrt{\frac{\log d}{n}}
+\text{a $\delta$ term}.
$$
If $\Theta^*$ obeys the spikiness bound $\|\Theta^*\|_{\max}\le\alpha/d$ of Corollary 10.18 (square case $d_1=d_2=d$), this is $O(\alpha\sqrt{(d\log d)/n})$. The choice
$$
\lambda_n
=C'(\sigma+\alpha)\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac{d\log d}{n}}+\delta\Bigr)
$$
therefore satisfies the hypothesis of (b) with high probability, and part (b) delivers
$$
\|\widehat\Theta-\Theta^*\|_{\mathrm{F}}
\lesssim
(\sigma+\alpha)\sqrt{\frac{r d\log d}{n}},
$$
the same Frobenius rate as Corollary 10.18.
:::
